solution: Section 13.1 defines an amine as ammonia with one, two or three hydrogen atoms replaced by alkyl or aryl groups, so the nitrogen of a primary amine \(\mathrm{R-NH_2}\) keeps the bonding pattern of the nitrogen in \(\mathrm{NH_3}\): three \(\sigma\) bonds (one to R, two to H) plus one lone pair. Four electron domains around nitrogen require four equivalent hybrid orbitals, that is \(sp^3\). Testing the alternatives: \(sp\) provides only two hybrid orbitals and \(sp^2\) only three, so neither can accommodate three bond pairs and a lone pair; \(sp^3d\) needs five domains and vacant d orbitals, which a second-period element such as nitrogen does not have. Hence the nitrogen is \(sp^3\) hybridised, consistent with the pyramidal amine structures drawn throughout the chapter. [Note: this chapter does not itself state the hybridisation of nitrogen in amines anywhere; the answer follows from the chapter's own definition of an amine as an \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) derivative together with the hybridisation rules from Std XI chemical bonding.]

Isobutylamine is \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-CH_2-NH_2}\). Section 13.1 classifies amines by the NUMBER of alkyl or aryl groups attached directly to the nitrogen atom, and the 'Remember...' box makes the point explicitly: amines are classified this way and not by the nature of the carbon carrying the functional group, so 'isopropyl amine is \(1^\circ\) amine, but isopropyl alcohol is \(2^\circ\) alcohol'. In isobutylamine exactly one alkyl group (the isobutyl group) is bonded to nitrogen, which leaves two N-H bonds. Branching in the carbon chain is therefore irrelevant to the classification. A secondary amine would carry two groups on nitrogen and a tertiary amine three, and a quaternary ammonium salt has four groups on a positively charged nitrogen with no N-H at all - none of which describes this molecule. Isobutylamine is a primary amine.

All four compounds are \(\mathrm{C_4H_{11}N}\) primary amines, so each has two N-H bonds available for the intermolecular hydrogen bonding described in section 13.4.1 and the comparison turns on the rest of the intermolecular attraction rather than on amine class. Table 13.3 tabulates two of these isomers directly: the unbranched \(\mathrm{n\text{-}C_4H_9NH_2}\) boils at 350.8 K while the fully branched \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-NH_2}\) (tert-butylamine) boils at 318.15 K, a fall of 32.6 K for the same molar mass 73. Branching makes the molecule more compact, reduces the surface over which neighbouring molecules touch, and so weakens the attraction between them. sec-Butylamine and isobutylamine are singly branched and therefore lie between these two extremes. The unbranched isomer, n-butylamine, has the highest boiling point of the four. [Note: the book tabulates only the n- and tert- isomers; the placement of the two singly branched isomers follows from the same branching argument, not from a printed value.]

Section 13.5 states that the smaller the \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) value the stronger the base, so the answer is simply the smallest tabulated \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) among the four. Table 13.4 gives ammonia 4.75, methanamine (methylamine) 3.38, N,N-dimethylmethanamine (trimethylamine) 4.22 and N-methylmethanamine (dimethylamine) 3.27. The smallest of these is 3.27, and every other option is printed with a larger value, so no other choice can be the strongest base. This also matches the chapter's own summary in bold that 'as per the observed \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) values of the aliphatic amines, secondary amines are the strongest bases', dimethylamine being the secondary amine here. The strongest base of the four is therefore dimethylamine.

Section 13.6.6(a) gives the reaction of an aliphatic primary amine with nitrous acid: \(\mathrm{R-NH_2} + \mathrm{HNO_2} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{(NaNO_2 + HCl)}]{273\text{-}278\ \mathrm{K}} [\mathrm{R-N_2^{\oplus}Cl^{\ominus}}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{R-OH} + \mathrm{N_2}\uparrow + \mathrm{HCl}\), and the accompanying text says the alkyl diazonium salt decomposes immediately in the solvent water so that 'nitrogen gas is liberated'. Nitrogen is therefore evolved from a primary amine. The chapter opens section 13.6.6 by stating that primary, secondary and tertiary amines react differently with nitrous acid and that only the primary-amine reactions will be considered, and it nowhere shows nitrogen being evolved from a secondary or a tertiary amine, so neither those two options nor the combined primary-and-secondary option is supported. It is the primary amine that produces \(\mathrm{N_2}\).

Section 13.6.5 states the answer directly: 'Aliphatic or aromatic primary amines on heating with chloroform give foul (offensive) smelling products called alkyl/aryl isocyanides or carbylamines. This reaction is a test for primary amines. Secondary and tertiary amines do not give this test.' The equation printed there is \(\mathrm{R-NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{R-NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\), and it needs the two hydrogen atoms of the \(\mathrm{-NH_2}\) group, which only a primary amine has. That same sentence rules out the secondary, the tertiary and the combined secondary-and-tertiary options. The carbylamine test is given by a primary amine.

Section 13.6.4 states that 'aliphatic and aromatic primary and secondary amines undergo acylation reaction. These amines contain replaceable hydrogen atoms (positively polarised H) on the nitrogen atom. These hydrogen atoms are replaced by acyl groups such as acetyl group.' Acylation by acetyl chloride therefore requires at least one hydrogen on nitrogen. Ethylamine \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2}\) is a primary aliphatic amine with two such hydrogens and diethylamine \(\mathrm{(CH_3-CH_2)_2NH}\) is a secondary amine with one, so both react; aniline \(\mathrm{C_6H_5-NH_2}\) is a primary aromatic amine and is covered by the same sentence, and the chapter in fact acetylates it in the p-bromoaniline and p-nitroaniline schemes. Triethylamine \(\mathrm{(CH_3-CH_2)_3N}\) is tertiary and carries no hydrogen on nitrogen at all, as the chapter's own 'Can you tell ?' box points out for tertiary amines. Triethylamine is the compound that does not react with acetyl chloride.

Hinsberg's reagent is benzenesulfonyl chloride \(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2Cl}\) (section 13.8). With ethylamine, a primary amine, it gives N-ethylbenzene sulfonamide, and the chapter states that 'the hydrogen attached to nitrogen in sulfonamide ethanamine (a primary amine) is strongly acidic. Hence it is soluble in alkali' - the product is labelled 'Soluble in alkali' in the printed scheme. With diethylamine, a secondary amine, it gives N,N-diethylbenzenesulfonamide, and the chapter says of that product that it 'does not contain any H-atom attached to nitrogen atom. Hence it is not acidic and does not dissolve in alkali.' Triethylamine and trimethylamine are tertiary amines with no hydrogen on nitrogen; the chapter's 'Can you tell ?' box asks why tertiary amines do not react with benzene sulfonyl chloride at all, so they form no sulfonamide to dissolve. Only ethylamine gives a product that dissolves in aqueous NaOH.

The first step is the Mendius reduction of section 13.3.3, \(\mathrm{R-C}\equiv\mathrm{N} + 4[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Na/C_2H_5OH}} \mathrm{R-CH_2-NH_2}\), so the intermediate labelled 'A' is ethylamine \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2}\). The second reagent, \(\mathrm{NaNO_2}\) with dilute HCl, generates nitrous acid in situ, and section 13.6.6(a) shows that an aliphatic primary amine so treated forms an alkyl diazonium salt which is 'very unstable' and 'decomposes immediately by reaction with solvent water', giving the corresponding alcohol together with nitrogen gas. The product labelled 'B' is therefore ethanol \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-OH}\). Of the other choices, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NH_2}\) is the intermediate 'A' of the first step and not the final product; \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-NO_2}\) would require a nitration, which neither reagent performs; and \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2N_2^{\oplus}Cl^{\ominus}}\) is exactly the unstable diazonium intermediate the chapter encloses in square brackets because it does not survive. The compound 'B' is ethanol.

Section 13.7.2 defines the azo linkage: in an azo compound 'two aromatic rings are joined through azo group \(\mathrm{-N=N-}\)'. p-Hydroxyazobenzene is the very compound the chapter names as the product of azo coupling between benzenediazonium chloride and phenol, and its printed structure shows two benzene rings joined by \(\mathrm{-N=N-}\), so it contains the azo linkage. Hydrazine \(\mathrm{H_2N-NH_2}\) has an N-N single bond and no aromatic rings; N-nitrosodiethylamine carries a nitroso group \(\mathrm{-N=O}\) on nitrogen, not a nitrogen-nitrogen double bond between two rings; and ethylenediamine \(\mathrm{H_2N-CH_2-CH_2-NH_2}\), listed in Table 13.2, has two separate amino groups with no nitrogen-nitrogen bond at all. p-Hydroxyazobenzene is the compound containing the azo linkage. [Note: hydrazine and N-nitrosodiethylamine are not discussed anywhere in this chapter; they are ruled out on their structures.]
